countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.intro: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland: world-class museums (mostly free), castles, moody highlands, pubs, and a calendar packed with festivals.

sp.text: Daffodils, bluebells (late Apr–mid May), lambing season, gardens waking up. Easter school holidays get busy. Chelsea Flower Show in late May.

su.text: Long days (light until 22:00+ in Scotland), festival season: Glastonbury, Wimbledon, Edinburgh Fringe. Peak prices, book early.

fa.text: Golden foliage, stags rutting in the Highlands, whisky and harvest season, Bonfire Night on Nov 5. Fewer crowds after early Sept.

wi.text: Short days (dark by 16:00), Christmas markets and pantomimes, Hogmanay in Edinburgh, cosy pubs with fires, cheapest flights in Jan–Feb.

items.d: The capital: royal palaces, the Thames, theatre, markets and dozens of free national museums. Give it at least 4–5 days.

items.w: Go at opening to see the Crown Jewels without queues
items.d: 900-year-old fortress holding the Crown Jewels, Beefeater tours and the White Tower armouries.

items.w: Walk the glass floor; check lift times online
items.d: Victorian bascule bridge with high-level walkways and glass floors over the Thames.
Coronation church since 1066, with the tombs of monarchs, Poets' Corner and Newton.

items.n: Houses of Parliament and Big Ben
items.w: UK residents get free tours; visitors can book paid tours on Saturdays
items.d: Gothic Revival parliament on the Thames; watch a debate from the public gallery for free.

items.w: Usually 11:00 Mon/Wed/Fri/Sun; daily in summer. Check schedule
items.d: Bearskin-hatted guards with a marching band at Buckingham Palace. Arrive 45 minutes early for a spot at the railings.
Rosetta Stone, Parthenon sculptures, Egyptian mummies, Sutton Hoo. Free entry.
Van Gogh's Sunflowers, Turner, Constable, da Vinci, on Trafalgar Square. Free.
Cathedral-like hall, dinosaurs and the blue whale skeleton. Ice rink outside in winter.
Design, fashion, sculpture and decorative arts; the café rooms alone are worth it.
Steam engines, the Apollo 10 capsule and hands-on galleries.

items.w: Free collection; climb to the viewing level
items.d: Modern art in a former power station on the South Bank, with a free viewing terrace.
Moving galleries on WWI, WWII and the Holocaust.
Wren's domed masterpiece; climb 528 steps for a view over the City.
Western Europe's tallest building with open-air viewing on floor 72.

items.w: Same-day discounts at the TKTS booth in Leicester Square
items.d: Musicals and plays in historic theatres; London's theatre scene rivals Broadway.

items.w: Open-air season roughly Apr–Oct; £5–10 standing tickets
items.d: Reconstructed Elizabethan theatre. Stand in the yard as a groundling for a few pounds.
London's oldest food market: cheese, oysters, scotch eggs, salt beef sandwiches.
Street food, vintage clothes and canal-side stalls.

items.w: Saturday is the big antiques day
items.d: Antiques, vintage and colourful Notting Hill houses.
Bangladeshi curry houses, street art and the famous salt beef bagels.
Eggs, bacon, sausage, beans, black pudding, toast. Essential.

items.w: Best at the seaside; try Whitby or Padstow
items.d: Battered cod or haddock with chips, mushy peas and vinegar.
Roast beef with Yorkshire puddings, potatoes and gravy in a proper pub.

items.w: Book at the Ritz, Fortnum's or a country hotel
items.d: Finger sandwiches, scones with clotted cream and jam, cakes and tea.

items.n: Cream tea in Devon or Cornwall
items.d: Scones, clotted cream and jam. Devon puts cream first, Cornwall jam first.
Crimped beef-and-swede pastry, the miner's lunch.

items.w: Try Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese or The Lamb & Flag
items.d: Real ale, Victorian interiors and pub quizzes.
Cellar-conditioned beer pulled by hand pump, served cool, not cold.
See Arsenal, Liverpool, Man United, City and others. Tickets are hard; use official club sales.

items.w: Spring blossom; Christmas at Kew light trail Nov–Jan
items.d: Glasshouses, a treetop walkway and 50,000 plants. Winter light trail is a highlight.
Henry VIII's palace with a famous maze and Tudor kitchens.

items.w: Book weeks ahead; Hogwarts in the Snow runs Nov–Jan
items.k: Warner Bros. Studio Tour London – The Making of Harry Potter
items.d: Original sets, costumes and the Hogwarts model.
Oldest occupied castle in the world, 45 minutes from London.

items.w: Summer solstice (Jun 21) and winter solstice open access
items.d: Neolithic stone circle. Solstice sunrise gatherings are free and unforgettable.
Largest stone circle in Britain, with a village built inside it and free access.
Georgian crescents, Roman Baths and the rooftop Thermae spa.
Bathe in natural thermal water with views over the abbey.
Dreaming spires, the Bodleian Library, punting and college quads.
King's College Chapel and punting along the Backs.
Glide past colleges in a flat-bottomed boat.

items.w: Wisteria in May; lavender at Snowshill in July
items.d: Honey-stone villages such as Bibury, Castle Combe and Bourton-on-the-Water.
Medieval walls, the Shambles and the vast York Minster.
One of Europe's largest Gothic cathedrals, with medieval stained glass.

items.w: Daffodils in March–April; misty walks in fall
items.d: Lakes, fells and Wordsworth country; hike Helvellyn or Catbells.
Gritstone edges, Chatsworth House and Bakewell pudding.
Grand stately home and gardens of the Dukes of Devonshire.
185 million years of rock; walk to Durdle Door and Lulworth Cove.

items.w: Late May and September beat the crowds
items.d: Coves, surf at Newquay, St Ives' art colony and fishing villages.

items.w: Walk the causeway at low tide
items.d: Tidal island castle reached on foot at low tide.
Giant biome greenhouses in a former clay pit.
Seaside pier, the Royal Pavilion and The Lanes.
Chalk cliffs; walk the clifftop path to the lighthouse.
Mother church of Anglicanism and site of Becket's murder.
"Loveliest castle in the world," set on a lake.
The Beatles, the Cavern Club, waterfront docks and football.
The Beatles' early venue, with live music every day.
Music history, the Northern Quarter, football at Old Trafford.

items.w: Goth weekends in Apr and late Oct
items.d: Abbey ruins that inspired Dracula, and top fish and chips.
Roman frontier; walk to Sycamore Gap and Housesteads fort.
Hogwarts' exterior in early Potter films, with broomstick lessons.
Spectacular show gardens; book well ahead.
Giant observation wheel on the South Bank.

items.w: Uber Boat by Thames Clippers is cheapest
items.d: Ride the Uber Boat by Thames Clippers from Westminster to Greenwich, passing the Tower, Tower Bridge and Canary Wharf. Uses a contactless card and costs a fraction of a tour boat.
Prime Meridian, the Cutty Sark and the Royal Observatory.
Castle on a volcanic rock, the Royal Mile and the Old Town's closes.

items.w: One O'Clock Gun daily except Sunday
items.d: Holds Scotland's crown jewels and the Stone of Destiny.
Extinct volcano right in the city, an easy 45-minute climb.
Mackintosh architecture, live music and the Kelvingrove museum.

items.w: Midges peak Jun–Aug; May and Sept are ideal
items.d: The wild north and west of Scotland: deep glens, mountain lochs, single-track roads and red deer. Best explored by car over a week or more.
Scotland's most dramatic glen, ringed by the Three Sisters and steeped in the 1692 massacre. Great hikes, waterfalls and the Clachaig Inn's climbers' bar.
Old Man of Storr, Quiraing, Fairy Pools and Neist Point.
The most photographed castle in Scotland, on a tiny tidal island where three lochs meet, reached by a stone footbridge. Rebuilt in the 1920s and a star of many films.
Deep, dark loch with Urquhart Castle and a monster legend.

items.w: Runs roughly Apr–Oct; book months ahead
items.d: Steam train over the Glenfinnan Viaduct (the "Hogwarts Express").
516-mile loop around the northern Highlands; rent a car.
Britain's only free-ranging reindeer.

items.w: Spirit of Speyside festival in late April–May
items.d: Tour Glenfiddich, Macallan, Laphroaig, Lagavulin; Islay for peat.
Scotland's national dish: spiced sheep's offal with oats in a casing, served with mashed turnip and potatoes, often with a whisky sauce. Better than it sounds.
A thick, creamy soup of smoked haddock, potatoes and onions from the fishing village of Cullen on the Moray coast. Perfect on a cold, wet day.
Skara Brae Neolithic village and the Ring of Brodgar.

items.n: Puffins on Lunga or Farne Islands
items.d: Boat trips land you among nesting puffins that waddle right past your feet. Lunga (Treshnish Isles) in Scotland and the Farnes off Northumberland are the best.
Castle, the Principality Stadium and the bay.
Climb Snowdon or take the mountain railway.
Cliff paths, beaches and the tiny city of St Davids.
Edward I's mighty castle and walled town.
Italianate fantasy village on the coast.
The fastest zipline in the world, over a slate quarry.

items.w: Early or late for no crowds
items.d: Around 40,000 interlocking basalt columns stepping into the sea, formed by an ancient lava flow (or by the giant Finn McCool, if you ask locally). UNESCO-listed.
Carrick-a-Rede rope bridge, Dunluce Castle, the Dark Hedges.
Titanic Belfast museum, murals and a black-taxi tour.
Interactive museum where the ship was built.
Studio tour in Banbridge and coastal filming spots.

items.w: Any grey afternoon; grab the front seat upstairs
items.d: Ride the top deck of the No. 11 or heritage Route 15 while rain streaks past Westminster and St Paul's. London at its most London.
Half the world's bluebells grow in Britain. Ashridge, Hole Park and Wytham Woods turn violet-blue.

items.w: Watch from the Clachaig Inn with a dram
items.d: Wind and horizontal rain tearing across the glen, waterfalls appearing on every slope, then a shaft of sunlight.
Pink avenues in Greenwich Park, Battersea Park and Kew.

items.n: Golden hour on the Seven Sisters cliffs
items.d: Chalk cliffs glowing over the Channel at Cuckmere Haven.
Free indoor garden at the top of the "Walkie-Talkie" skyscraper.
Underground bunker where Churchill ran WWII, preserved as it was left.
Overgrown Victorian Gothic cemetery with Karl Marx's tomb.
Ornate Victorian covered market (Diagon Alley in the first Potter film).
Narrowboats, waterside cafés and a towpath walk to Camden.
Stand with a foot in each hemisphere on 0° longitude.
The world's last surviving tea clipper.
Walk the Beatles' zebra crossing outside the studios.

items.n: Coal Drops Yard and King's Cross
items.d: Victorian coal sheds turned shopping and dining, plus Platform 9¾.
Turner Bequest, Pre-Raphaelites and British art since 1500.
Faces of British history, newly renovated.
An architect's eccentric house crammed with antiquities.
The Laughing Cavalier and Rococo treasures in a mansion.
Contemporary design in Holland Park.
Buses, trams and Tube trains in Covent Garden.
Ride the tiny underground Mail Rail train.
700-year-old nightly locking of the Tower of London.
Choral evensong at Westminster Abbey, St Paul's or King's College Chapel.
Stand-up in the city that invented the panel show.
Legendary Soho jazz club since 1959.
FA Cup final, NFL London games and stadium concerts.
The 82,000-seat home of English rugby. Autumn internationals and Six Nations matches come with a famously friendly crowd and a car-park picnic culture.
Britain's most famous steeplechase.

items.w: Old Course ballot opens days ahead
items.d: The home of golf; the Old Course is public via a daily ballot.
Riverside walk past every London landmark.
154 km from Glasgow to Fort William.
1,014 km of cliffs, coves and pasties; do a section.
Cruise the canals at 4 mph, through locks and to canalside pubs.
Military jets fly low through the valleys.
A rolling line of white chalk cliffs on the South Downs Way. Walk from Cuckmere Haven to Birling Gap and on to the red-and-white lighthouse below Beachy Head.
Stone barns, limestone pavements and Malham Cove.
Limestone cliff and pavement (Harry Potter location).
Ponies wander free through heath and villages.
A wild moorland plateau of granite tors, prehistoric stone rows, wild ponies and old stone bridges. One of the few places in England where wild camping is allowed in parts.
Chalk stacks at the eastern end of the Jurassic Coast near Studland. An easy clifftop walk with views across to the Isle of Wight.
Scotland's largest loch, 45 minutes from Glasgow.
The world's largest colony of northern gannets, about 150,000 birds, turning the volcanic rock white. Boat trips leave from North Berwick.
Puffins and gannets on English cliffs.
Serpentine rocks and turquoise water.
Art colony with Tate St Ives and beaches.
Fishing village famous for its harbour lights.
A cobbled hilltop town in East Sussex with crooked Tudor houses, smugglers' inns and Mermaid Street, one of the prettiest streets in England.
One of England's best-preserved medieval wool towns, with more than 300 listed buildings and wonky half-timbered houses (a Harry Potter filming location).
Shakespeare's birthplace and the Royal Shakespeare Company.
A Roman and medieval city with the most complete city walls in Britain and the Rows, two-tiered galleried shopping streets dating from the 1200s.
Norman cathedral and castle above the river.
Medieval lanes and Norfolk Broads gateway.
Banksy's hometown, the SS Great Britain and Clifton Bridge.
Ancient capital with King Arthur's Round Table.
Tallest spire in Britain and the best Magna Carta.
Gateway to the Highlands, with Stirling Castle on its crag, the Wallace Monument and the battlefields of Stirling Bridge and Bannockburn.
University town, cathedral ruins and golf.
The Highland capital on the River Ness, base for Loch Ness, Culloden battlefield, Cawdor Castle and the North Coast 500.
Tobermory's brightly painted harbour fronts an island famous for white-tailed sea eagles, otters and boat trips to Staffa and Iona.
The whisky island: nine working distilleries including Laphroaig, Lagavulin, Ardbeg and Bowmore, producing Scotland's smokiest, peatiest drams.
Victorian resort town with a salmon ladder.
Victorian seaside resort with a pier.
A tiny Welsh border town with more than 20 secondhand bookshops, and host of the famous Hay Festival of literature every late May.
Edward I's mighty 13th-century fortress with polygonal towers, built to subdue the Welsh and used for the investiture of Princes of Wales.
Churchill's birthplace, Baroque palace.
A Baroque palace in the Yorkshire countryside used in Brideshead Revisited and Bridgerton, with lakes, temples and a spectacular Christmas display.
A huge castle on a basalt outcrop above one of England's finest beaches, with views to Lindisfarne and the Farne Islands.
A tidal island cradle of English Christianity with a ruined priory and a small castle. The causeway floods twice a day, so check tide tables.
Dramatic clifftop ruins on a headland near Stonehaven, where the Scottish crown jewels were hidden from Cromwell's army.
A ruined castle on the shore of Loch Ness, with a grand tower overlooking the dark water. Best viewed from a boat trip.
Two 30 m stainless-steel horse heads by Andy Scott near Falkirk, celebrating Scotland's working horses. Lit up spectacularly after dark.
The world's only rotating boat lift, swinging canal boats 35 m between two canals. Take the boat ride through it.
Remarkably preserved Roman bathing complex fed by Britain's only natural hot springs. Summer evening torchlit openings are atmospheric.
Birthplace of the Industrial Revolution.
Vita Sackville-West's romantic garden rooms around an Elizabethan tower, including the famous all-White Garden.
A grand National Trust garden in North Wales famous for its 55 m laburnum arch, which turns into a golden tunnel in late May.
A huge open-air living museum recreating northern England in the 1820s, 1900s and 1950s, with trams, a colliery, shops and a working pub.
The world's largest railway museum, with record-breaking Mallard, the Japanese Bullet Train and royal carriages. Free entry.
Dalí's Christ of St John of the Cross.
Zaha Hadid's zigzag building on the Clyde, full of trams, cars and a recreated Glasgow street, with a tall ship moored outside. Free entry.
Kengo Kuma's ship-like design museum on Dundee's waterfront, with a reconstructed Charles Rennie Mackintosh tearoom.
The royal family's floating palace.
From Dolly the cloned sheep to Viking hoards and the Lewis chessmen. Free, with a rooftop terrace overlooking Edinburgh Castle.

items.k: St Fagans National Museum of History
items.d: A free open-air museum near Cardiff with 40 rebuilt historic Welsh buildings, from Iron Age roundhouses to a 1940s prefab.
Descend 90 m underground with former miners in a real coal mine in Blaenavon. Free entry, and an unforgettable experience.
Explore the dark chambers beneath South Bridge where the city's poorest once lived, with tales of plague and hauntings.
Scottish folk dancing with a caller.

items.n: Country walk ending at a pub
items.d: Classic English country walk ending at a pub.
A ten-day festival of books and ideas in late May and early June, with authors, politicians and scientists.
Four days of jump racing in March, with the Gold Cup on Friday and roaring Irish crowds.
Chase a cheese down a near-vertical hill.
Dawn gatherings on the Tor for Beltane, with views over the Somerset Levels and a pagan festival atmosphere in town.
A Cockney classic: minced-beef pie with mashed potato and green "liquor" parsley sauce. Try M. Manze's on Tower Bridge Road.

items.n: Chicken tikka masala and Birmingham balti
items.d: Britain's adopted national dishes. Birmingham's Balti Triangle claims the balti, cooked fast in a steel bowl.
A pub plate of hearty bread, Cheddar, pickle, apple and pickled onions. Best with a pint in a country pub garden.
A hard- or soft-boiled egg wrapped in sausage meat, breaded and fried. Gastropubs serve them warm with runny yolks.
Almond frangipane over jam in a pastry case, from the Derbyshire town of Bakewell, where shops dispute who invented the original "pudding."
Welsh rarebit is cheese and ale sauce grilled on toast. Pair it with Welsh cakes, griddled currant scones.
Taste Stilton, mature Cheddar, Wensleydale and Stinking Bishop at a cheesemonger like Neal's Yard Dairy.
Spiced, fruited buns marked with a cross, traditionally eaten toasted with butter on Good Friday.
West coast seafood at its best: oak-smoked salmon, langoustines and scallops in harbour towns like Oban and Ullapool.
Haddock hot-smoked over hardwood in barrels in the fishing town of Arbroath. Eat it warm straight from the smokehouse.

items.n: Irn-Bru and a deep-fried Mars bar
items.d: Irn-Bru is Scotland's bright orange soda, outselling Coke. The deep-fried Mars bar is an infamous chip-shop dare.
London's gin boom: tour Sipsmith, Beefeater or the City of London Distillery and mix your own gin.
Southern England's chalk soils produce award-winning sparkling wine. Tour Nyetimber, Ridgeview or Chapel Down.
Spend a night in a free, unlocked mountain shelter in the Highlands. Bring your own sleeping bag, food and firewood.
Stay in a lighthouse keeper's cottage.
Sleep in a stately home turned hotel, like Cliveden or Gleneagles, with afternoon tea and estate walks.
Harrods' food halls and Egyptian escalator, and Liberty's Tudor-revival store full of prints and fabrics.
A Sunday-morning flower market in East London where traders shout out their deals among independent shops.
The home of bespoke tailoring and traditional shirtmakers, where you can order a suit fitted over several visits.
Regency shopping arcade with beadles.

items.w: Open only mid-July to end of September
items.d: The monarch's London home opens its State Rooms each summer while the King is away.
England's highest peak (978 m). The classic route from Wasdale Head is a steep 5–6 hour round trip over boulder fields to a stony summit with views to Scotland and the Isle of Man on clear days.
Open-air theatre carved into cliffs above the sea.

items.w: Late June; skips some years. Tickets sell out in minutes in October
items.d: The biggest greenfield music festival in the world.

items.w: Late June–mid July; join "The Queue" for same-day tickets
items.d: Grass-court tennis with strawberries and cream.
Europe's largest street carnival, Caribbean music and food.
The King's birthday parade with an RAF flypast.
Formula 1 at the circuit that hosted the first-ever world championship race in 1950. Huge crowds, campsites, and the fastest corners on the calendar at Maggotts and Becketts.
World's largest arts festival, thousands of comedy and theatre shows.
Massed pipes and drums on the castle esplanade.
Britain's highest mountain (1,345 m).
The whole skyline turns gold while Londoners picnic with cheap wine on the grass.
The sun barely sets, leaving an all-night twilight over the sea cliffs.
Hills blanketed in purple heather; walk from Goathland or Hutton-le-Hole.

items.n: Proms at the Royal Albert Hall
items.d: Eight weeks of classical concerts; Last Night of the Proms in September.
Test match at the "home of cricket."
Top hats, fascinators and royal racing.
Golf's oldest major; 2027 returns to St Andrews.
Wild swimming in North London's ponds.
Wainwright's 300 km walk across England.

items.n: Gorge walking in Wales or Scotland
items.d: Scramble up rivers and jump into pools.
Britain's surf capital in Newquay, with consistent Atlantic swell, surf schools and board hire. The water is cold year-round, so a thick wetsuit is a must.
Paddle under sea arches and into caves along the Pembrokeshire coast, or try coasteering (scrambling and cliff-jumping along the shoreline), which was invented here.
Basalt sea cave that inspired Mendelssohn.
White sand and turquoise water like the Caribbean, at 15°C.
A 137 m sandstone sea stack off Orkney's Hoy island. Watch it from the ferry to Stromness or hike out to the clifftop viewpoint.
Britain's largest protected wetland: 200 km of rivers and lakes. Rent a day boat or cabin cruiser and stop at waterside pubs and windmills.
Mass dawn ascents of 100+ balloons.
An island off the south coast with the chalk Needles, Osborne House (Queen Victoria's retreat), dinosaur beaches and Britain's sailing capital at Cowes.
A walled seaside town of pastel Georgian houses above two sandy beaches in Pembrokeshire, with boat trips to the monks' island of Caldey.
The real "Downton Abbey," a Victorian Jacobethan mansion in Hampshire. Opens only on limited summer dates and some holidays; book well ahead.

items.n: Fringe street performers on the Royal Mile
items.d: During the Fringe, the Royal Mile becomes a free street stage of jugglers, acrobats and actors flyering for their shows.
Traditional gatherings with caber tossing, hammer throwing, tug-of-war, Highland dancing and massed pipe bands. Braemar in September is attended by the royal family.
Watch border collies herd sheep across the fells with whistled commands at Lake District shows in late summer.
County shows with cattle and cakes.
A big rock and pop festival on the island in June, with a long history including Jimi Hendrix's 1970 performance.
Twin festivals over the August bank holiday weekend with the same rock, indie and hip-hop line-up.
Britain's biggest heavy metal festival at Donington Park each June.
One of the world's biggest sailing regattas, with hundreds of races in the Solent and lively evening parties.
A five-day rowing event on the Thames in early July, famous for its strict dress code of blazers and boaters.
Supercars, F1 cars and legends tackle a hill climb up the Duke of Richmond's drive, with paddocks you can walk through.
One of the world's largest Pride parades, through central London with Trafalgar Square stages.
The quintessential English summer treat, served by the tonne at Wimbledon.
A fruity gin-based summer cup, served with lemonade, cucumber, mint and strawberries at Wimbledon, Henley and garden parties.
Torchlit processions and burning effigies, Britain's wildest Bonfire Night.
Each autumn, stags roar, posture and clash antlers to win hinds. Glen Etive, Glen Torridon and the Isle of Rum are the best places to hear the bellowing echo around the hills.
Visible on strong nights from Caithness and Shetland.

items.n: Fog over the Thames at dawn
items.d: Walk the South Bank early when mist swallows the bridges and Big Ben's tower fades into grey.

items.w: Mid–late October; illuminated trail in Dec
items.d: Japanese maples in fiery reds and oranges, one of Britain's great autumn displays.
Tens of thousands of starlings swirling in shape-shifting clouds before roosting.

items.n: Pub fire on a wet winter night
items.d: Muddy boots off, a pint of bitter and a crackling log fire after a rainy country walk.
England's largest dark-sky park; the Milky Way and occasional aurora.
An award-winning woodland light and sound show in Faskally Wood near Pitlochry each October. Tickets sell out early.
Vintage motor racing where everyone dresses in pre-1966 fashion, with period cars, planes and costume parties.
The national service at the Cenotaph in Whitehall with the King, veterans' march-past and two minutes of silence.
The largest Diwali celebration outside India, with a lights switch-on and fireworks along the Golden Mile.
A light art festival that projects installations onto Durham's cathedral and streets, usually every two years in November.
10 km of seaside lights along the Promenade from late August to early January, a British tradition since 1879.

items.n: Christmas lights on Oxford and Regent Streets
items.d: Lights, window displays and Winter Wonderland in Hyde Park.
Rides, an ice rink and Bavarian-style bars.
Uniquely British comic family theatre with audience heckling.

items.n: New Year's Eve fireworks on the Thames
items.d: Fireworks over the London Eye. Tickets required for the riverside.
Torchlight procession, street party and fireworks over the castle.
Fire festival where costumed "Vikings" burn a longship.
Haggis, whisky and poetry in honour of Robert Burns.
Small but fun Scottish ski areas; see the free-roaming reindeer herd.
Rugby with packed pubs and anthems.
Honey-stone cottages and dry-stone walls under fresh snow, with a fire in the pub.
Low winter sun through the stones on a frosty morning.
Thousands of seal pups on the beach.
Snowdrop walks at Painswick and Welford Park.
Wooden chalets selling crafts and mulled wine spread around Bath Abbey and the Roman Baths, against a backdrop of Georgian stone.
On Shrove Tuesday, runners race through Olney in Buckinghamshire tossing pancakes in frying pans, a tradition since 1445.
At midnight on Hogmanay, locals swing flaming balls of wire and rags around their heads down the High Street before hurling them into the harbour.
Christmas staples: tiny pies of spiced dried fruit and a dense, brandy-flamed pudding served with custard.
Hot spiced cider served at winter markets and pubs, especially in the West Country.

countries.name: Ireland
countries.intro: Green landscapes, cliffs, music-filled pubs and friendly towns. Compact enough for a road trip around the island.

sp.text: Lambs, wildflowers and St Patrick's Day (Mar 17). Good value before June.

su.text: Long days (dark at 22:30), festivals, and the best chance of dry hiking weather. Busiest season.

fa.text: Quieter roads, harvest food festivals, Galway Oyster Festival, Halloween's birthplace.

wi.text: Wet and windy but cosy: trad music by the fire, Newgrange solstice, Christmas in Dublin.

items.d: Georgian squares, Trinity College, pubs and literary history.

items.n: Book of Kells and Trinity College
items.d: 9th-century illuminated gospels and the Long Room library.
Learn to pour the perfect pint with a rooftop view.

items.n: Temple Bar pubs and live music
items.d: Lively pub district. Locals prefer The Brazen Head or Kehoe's.
Prison where the 1916 Rising leaders were executed.
How 10 million people left Ireland and shaped the world.
Jameson's original 1780 distillery in Smithfield, with guided tours, whiskey blending classes and a lively bar.
Fishing village with a cliff walk and seafood.
Monastic site and lakes in the Wicklow Mountains.

items.w: Winter solstice lottery for chamber access Dec 18–23
items.d: 5,200-year-old passage tomb lit by the solstice sunrise.
214 m sea cliffs; walk the coastal trail from Doolin.
Limestone moonscape and the Poulnabrone dolmen.
Traditional music capital, ferries to the Aran Islands.
Bike Inis Mór to the cliff fort of Dún Aonghasa.

items.w: Arts Festival in July; Oyster Festival late Sept
items.d: Bohemian city of buskers, pubs and festivals.
Bogs, mountains and Kylemore Abbey.
Neo-Gothic abbey reflected in a lake.
A 2,500 km signposted route along the west coast from Donegal to Cork, linking cliffs, beaches, peninsulas and music towns.
Classic coastal loop around the Iveragh Peninsula.
Slea Head Drive, beaches and pubs that double as hardware shops.
Lakes, Muckross House and the Gap of Dunloe by jaunting car.
Medieval cathedral complex on a limestone rock.
Kiss the Blarney Stone for the gift of the gab.
Ireland's food capital and its covered market.
Colourful harbour town known for seafood.
Medieval city with a castle and Smithwick's brewery.
Among the highest sea cliffs in Europe.
Cold-water surfing on Atlantic swell with surf schools, wetsuit hire and post-surf pints. Autumn has the best waves.
Parade and celebrations across the country.
Fiddles, bodhráns and tin whistles in a pub corner.
Lamb stew with brown soda bread and butter.
Rashers, sausages, eggs, white and black pudding, beans, tomato and soda bread. Fuel for a day of hiking.
Invented at Foynes flying-boat terminal in 1943.
Spend a night in a real castle like Ashford, Dromoland or Kilkea, with falconry, archery and grand dining rooms.
Sun, sideways rain, hail and a double rainbow within an hour. It's part of the experience.
Ireland's showers make rainbows almost daily over bogs and mountains.
Monastic round tower rising out of fog by the Upper Lake.
Coconut-scented gorse covering hillsides.

items.n: Winter swim at the Forty Foot
items.d: Locals plunge into the Irish Sea year-round, packed on Christmas morning.
Cast-iron footbridge over the Liffey.
Ireland's largest cathedral, founded beside a well where St Patrick baptised converts. Jonathan Swift was dean and is buried here.
Medieval crypt with a mummified cat and rat.
Seat of British rule for 700 years.
Wild fallow deer in Europe's largest city park.
Ireland's oldest public library, with reading cages.
Street musicians and Bewley's café.
Free museum with Iron Age bog bodies, the Tara Brooch, Ardagh Chalice and dazzling Celtic gold.
A Georgian townhouse crammed with donated objects telling the story of 20th-century Dublin, on a funny guided tour.
Learn the history of Irish whiskey opposite Trinity College, finishing with a tasting of several styles.
Inside the General Post Office, the rebels' headquarters during the 1916 Easter Rising, with immersive exhibits.
Actors perform Joyce, Beckett and Behan as they lead you between historic pubs.
Two of the world's great links courses, among dunes beside the Atlantic.
Watch border collies herd sheep on a working farm, with Kissane's on the Ring of Kerry being the best-known.

items.w: Reek Sunday (last Sunday of July) pilgrimage
items.d: Ireland's holy mountain above Clew Bay, where St Patrick fasted for 40 days. A steep scree climb with sea views, made barefoot by some pilgrims on Reek Sunday.
A 42 km traffic-free bike path along an old railway from Westport to Achill, with views over Clew Bay.
Cycle 46 km of old railway over viaducts and through a tunnel between Waterford city and Dungarvan.
Ireland's oldest waymarked trail, 130 km through the mountains south of Dublin, past Glendalough.
Ireland's largest island, with Keem Bay beach, the Atlantic Drive and the deserted village on Slievemore.
Hike 18 km along the cliff tops from Doolin to Hag's Head, away from the visitor centre crowds.
Seaside saunas have boomed along the coast; sweat, then plunge into the cold Atlantic.
A narrow mountain pass in Killarney with lakes and stone bridges, travelled by jaunting car, bike or on foot, ending in a boat across the lakes.
A remote Donegal park with a Victorian castle on a lake, walled gardens and reintroduced golden eagles.
Flat-topped mountain of Yeats country.
A quieter, wilder alternative to the Ring of Kerry, with Ireland's only cable car to Dursey Island.
Ireland's most southwesterly point, with a signal station reached by a bridge over a deep gorge.
A lighthouse on a dramatic peninsula between two sea loughs. You can stay in the keepers' cottages.
A UNESCO Global Geopark of coves, cliffs and old copper mines along the Waterford coast.
A dark lake with a white sand beach, owned by the Guinness family, below the Sally Gap in Wicklow.
A Georgian town with tree-lined riverside streets and Matt Molloy's pub, famous for traditional music.
A colourful Kerry town known for its restaurants, between the Ring of Kerry and the Ring of Beara.
The colourful harbour town that was the Titanic's last port of call and where millions of emigrants left Ireland.
A village of thatched cottages and medieval abbeys, often called Ireland's prettiest village.
Yeats country and surfing at Strandhill.
A 6th-century monastic site on the River Shannon with round towers, high crosses and ruined churches.
A seaside village south of Dublin with castles, Sorrento Point views and celebrity residents.
County Clare's capital and a hub of traditional music, with sessions in many pubs.
A restored 15th-century castle and a recreated village. Join the medieval banquet with mead and harp music.
Largest Norman castle (Braveheart).
The ancient seat of Ireland's high kings, with earthworks and the Stone of Destiny on a hilltop.
A Palladian mansion with Italian and Japanese gardens and Ireland's highest waterfall nearby.
A Victorian mansion on the lake shore in Killarney National Park, with traditional farms nearby.
A 16th-century tower house on Galway Bay near Kinvara, with medieval banquets in summer.
The home of Daniel O'Connell, "the Liberator," set beside a beautiful beach on the Ring of Kerry.
Creamy fish chowder with brown bread.
A traditional potato pancake made from grated and mashed potato, served with meats or butter.

items.n: Kinsale mussels and Dublin Bay prawns
items.d: Kinsale is Ireland's gourmet capital; order mussels in cream and Dublin Bay prawns in garlic butter.
Award-winning cheeses like Gubbeen, Cashel Blue and Durrus, from small family farms.

items.n: Pint of Guinness in a real pub
items.d: Drink a perfectly poured pint in an old Dublin pub like Mulligan's, Kehoe's or Toner's, with no TV.
Ireland's traditional, once-illegal spirit, distilled from potatoes or grain. Now legal and sold by craft distillers.
A small craft distillery making whiskey, gin and vodka in the Kerry fishing town of Dingle.
Stay in a lighthouse keeper's cottage at places like Fanad, Wicklow Head or Loop Head through the Great Lighthouses of Ireland.
Rent a whitewashed thatched cottage in the west of Ireland with a turf fire and views.
Monastic beehive huts on a sea rock (Star Wars location).
Ancient fair where a wild goat is crowned king.
Long golden evenings on the Dingle and Iveragh peninsulas.
In late summer, the narrow roads of the Dingle Peninsula are lined with walls of red-and-purple fuchsia.
Hurling and Gaelic football, the world's fastest field sport.
Edwardian costumes and Ulysses readings.
A week-long summer festival of racing in late July and early August, as much a social party as a sporting event.
Paddle Dingle Harbour and the coast below the cliffs, where dolphins and seals often appear.
Ireland's highest mountain (1,038 m) in the MacGillycuddy's Reeks. The Devil's Ladder route is the classic; go with a guide in poor weather.
World's largest Irish music festival.
Two weeks of theatre, music, street spectacle and art in late July that fill Galway's streets.
Ireland's biggest music and arts festival on a country estate in late August.
Oyster shucking contests and parties.
Halloween started as Samhain here; the Púca festival relights ancient fires.
Native flat oysters from Galway Bay, eaten with brown bread and a pint of stout. Best during the September festival.

items.n: Atlantic storm on the Cliffs of Moher
items.w: Oct–Feb; stay well back from the edge
items.d: Gale-force wind sending spray up the 200 m cliffs, then a rainbow over the Aran Islands minutes later.

items.n: Turf fire smoke in a village
items.d: The smell of burning peat drifting from cottage chimneys on a cold evening.
Ireland's northernmost point and the best spot in the country to see the aurora on strong nights.
A month-long festival of music and dancing in September, with a traditional matchmaker.
An internationally known festival staging rare and forgotten operas each autumn.
Europe's oldest specialist theatre festival, with Irish and international productions.
Jazz across pubs, clubs and venues over the October bank holiday weekend.
A Dublin dish of sausages, bacon and potatoes slow-cooked in stock. Hearty pub food.
A fruit loaf eaten at Halloween, with a ring hidden inside: whoever finds it will marry within the year.
Lights on Grafton Street and markets.
A national holiday on February 1 celebrating Ireland's female patron saint and the start of spring, with woven rush crosses.

countries.name: France
countries.intro: The world's most-visited country: Paris, Loire châteaux, Provence lavender, Alpine skiing, the Riviera, Normandy beaches and some of the planet's best food and wine.

sp.text: Paris blossoms, Easter, mild Provence, Cannes Film Festival and the Monaco GP in May. Shoulder-season prices.

su.text: Lavender (late Jun–mid Jul), Riviera beaches, Tour de France, Bastille Day. Parisians leave in August; many small shops close.

fa.text: Grape harvests (Sept–Oct), Beaujolais Nouveau (3rd Thursday in Nov), golden Loire and Burgundy, warm sea in Sept.

wi.text: Alpine skiing, Strasbourg Christmas markets, Menton Lemon Festival and Nice Carnival in Feb, Paris without crowds.

items.d: Café terraces, boulevards, museums and neighbourhoods to wander for days.

items.w: Book the summit online; sparkles hourly after dark for 5 minutes
items.d: Climb or lift to the top; picnic on the Champ de Mars.

items.w: Book a slot; Friday night openings; closed Tuesdays
items.d: Mona Lisa, Venus de Milo, Winged Victory and 35,000 works.
Impressionists in a Belle Époque railway station; look out through the clock window.
Monet's oval rooms of Water Lilies.
The Thinker and The Kiss in a rose garden.

items.w: Check reopening; closed for renovation from 2025 to around 2030
items.d: Paris's inside-out modern art centre, with its pipes and escalators on the outside. Closed for renovation from 2025 to about 2030; the collection is on loan elsewhere.

items.w: Reopened December 2024; free, reserve a time
items.d: Restored Gothic cathedral after the 2019 fire.
Walls of 13th-century stained glass.
Climb for views down the Champs-Élysées.
Hilltop village of painters, cabarets and the white basilica.
Medieval lanes, Place des Vosges, falafel on Rue des Rosiers.
Shakespeare and Company, the Sorbonne and literary cafés.
Paris's favourite park, with toy sailboats.
Tunnels lined with the bones of six million people.
Jim Morrison, Oscar Wilde, Edith Piaf and Chopin.
Bateaux Mouches or a dinner cruise past illuminated monuments.
The original red-windmill cabaret at the foot of Montmartre, with can-can dancers, feathers and champagne.

items.w: Tour by day or see a ballet
items.d: Gilded opera house that inspired the Phantom of the Opera.
Steak frites, duck confit and crème brûlée.

items.n: Croissant and pain au chocolat from a boulangerie
items.d: Morning ritual. Try the annual "best croissant" winners.

items.n: Macarons at Ladurée or Pierre Hermé
items.d: Delicate almond meringue sandwiches.
France has more than 1,000 cheeses: Comté, Brie de Meaux, Roquefort, Époisses.
Brittany's buckwheat galettes filled with ham, egg and cheese, followed by a sweet butter-sugar crêpe and a bowl of cider.
Raw chopped beef mixed with capers, shallots and egg yolk, served with fries. A bistro classic.
Snails in garlic and parsley butter.

items.n: Marché aux Puces and food markets
items.d: Flea markets and markets like Aligre and Rue Cler.
Hall of Mirrors, the gardens and Marie Antoinette's hamlet.

items.w: Open April–Oct; irises and wisteria in May
items.d: Monet's lily pond and Japanese bridge.
Two parks, Disneyland and Walt Disney Studios (expanded with a new Frozen land), 40 minutes east of Paris by RER.
A royal palace used by French kings for eight centuries, with Napoleon's throne room and a vast forest for walking and climbing.
The French Open tennis Grand Slam on red clay, from late May to early June.
Abbey island rising from tidal flats.
Omaha Beach, Pointe du Hoc and the American Cemetery.

items.w: Check status; due to travel to the British Museum 2026–27
items.d: 70-metre embroidered story of 1066.
White chalk cliffs with sea arches and a needle on the Normandy coast, painted by Monet. Walk the cliff paths on both sides.
A painterly harbour of tall, narrow houses around the Vieux Bassin, which inspired the Impressionists.
A walled corsair city on the Breton coast. Walk the ramparts and out to the tidal island of Grand Bé at low tide.
More than 3,000 standing stones in long rows, erected around 4500 BC. Some of the world's largest megalithic sites.
The Loire's largest château with a double-helix staircase.
The "Ladies' Château," spanning the River Cher on arches, with formal gardens and lavish Christmas decorations.
900 km of flat bike routes between châteaux.
Taste Sancerre, Vouvray and Chinon in cave cellars dug into the soft limestone along the river.
Elegant 18th-century city and wine capital.
Wine museum with a top-floor tasting.
Medieval wine village and grand cru estates.
Europe's highest sand dune, over 100 m, between the Atlantic and a pine forest near Arcachon. Climb it for sunset.
Oysters straight from the bay's huts.
Medieval town, cliff villages and canoeing.
Replica of 17,000-year-old cave paintings.
A pilgrimage village stacked up a cliff above the Alzou canyon, with chapels and a Black Madonna.
Fairy-tale walled city with 52 towers.
A three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge built around 50 AD. Swim and picnic in the river below in summer.
Hill towns, markets, rosé and light.
Papal Palace and the broken bridge.
A Provençal town with a Roman arena, Van Gogh painting sites and the Luma Arles tower by Gehry.
Hilltop villages and Roussillon's ochre cliffs.
An elegant town of fountains, the Cours Mirabeau, markets and Cézanne's studio and mountain.
France's oldest city: the Old Port, Notre-Dame de la Garde, the MuCEM museum and the Calanques.

items.w: Some trails close in high-fire risk days
items.d: Limestone inlets with turquoise water.
Marseille's famous fish stew, served in two courses with rouille and croutons. A proper one costs €60+.
Wild horses, flamingos and cowboys.
Promenade des Anglais and the old town.
Medieval hilltop villages: Èze has an exotic garden above the sea; Saint-Paul has art galleries and the Fondation Maeght.
Cannes for glamour on the Croisette; Antibes for its old town, ramparts and Picasso Museum.
Mountains and beaches; hike the GR20.
France's gastronomic capital, with Roman theatres, Renaissance Vieux Lyon and traboule passageways.
Rustic restaurants with quenelles and pink pralines.

items.w: Hospices de Beaune auction in Nov
items.d: Côte d'Or wine villages and Beaune.
Cellar tours at Moët, Veuve Clicquot and Taittinger.
Alsace's capital: the half-timbered Petite France quarter, the soaring cathedral and the EU Parliament.
A canal-lined Alsace town of brightly painted half-timbered houses ("Little Venice").
Alsatian specialities: thin flatbread with cream and bacon, and sauerkraut piled with sausages and pork.
The "Venice of the Alps," with canals and flower boxes, on a clear turquoise lake ringed by mountains.
The birthplace of mountaineering, under Western Europe's highest mountain (4,806 m). Lively in every season.
A cable car to 3,842 m, with the "Step into the Void" glass box and views of Mont Blanc.
The world's largest linked ski area: 600 km of pistes connecting Courchevel, Méribel and Val Thorens.
High-altitude, snow-sure skiing with a season stretching from late November to early May.

items.n: Nantes and Les Machines de l'île
items.k: Machines of the Isle of Nantes
items.d: Ride a 12 m mechanical elephant and see steampunk machines in Nantes' old shipyards.

items.w: Braderie flea market 1st weekend of Sept
items.d: A lively Flemish-French city with Grand Place, waffles from Méert and Europe's largest flea market each September.

items.w: Any drizzly day; duck into a covered passage
items.d: Wet cobbles reflecting street lamps, umbrellas on the Pont des Arts, then coffee under the glass roofs of Galerie Vivienne.

items.w: Blows 3–10 days at a time, mainly winter–spring
items.d: A cold north wind that scrubs the sky to deep blue and makes the light painters chased.
In mid-May, red poppies fill the fields and olive groves of the Luberon and the Alpilles.
Provence's first blossom: almond trees in February, cherries in the Luberon in April.
The bay floods "at the speed of a galloping horse."
Bridges and the Eiffel Tower sparkling from the quays.
Huge Picasso collection in a Marais mansion.
Medieval art and the Lady and the Unicorn tapestries.
Gehry's glass-sail museum in the Bois de Boulogne.
Pinault contemporary art under a domed rotunda.
A free museum of Paris history in two Marais mansions, with shop signs, Proust's bedroom and the Revolution.
The world's largest Monet collection, including Impression, Sunrise, in a mansion near the Bois de Boulogne.
A Belle Époque mansion with Italian Renaissance art and one of the city's prettiest tea rooms.
Immersive projections of famous artists.
Napoleon's giant tomb under a golden dome.
Foucault's pendulum and tombs of Voltaire and Hugo.

items.n: Palais Royal and Colonnes de Buren
items.d: Striped columns and a hidden garden.
Paris's 19th-century glass-roofed arcades, with mosaic floors, bookshops and cafés.
An iron-bridged canal with locks, plane trees and hip bars; Parisians picnic along its edge.
Elevated park that inspired the High Line.
A hilly park in northeast Paris with cliffs, a waterfall, a suspension bridge and a temple on a rock.
Formal garden between the Louvre and Concorde.
The oldest planned square in Paris (1612), with red-brick arcades. Victor Hugo's house is on one corner.
The modern home of the Paris Opera, with big productions at lower prices than the Palais Garnier.
Business district with a giant hollow cube.
The first Gothic church and burial place of almost every French king and queen.
Baguette, cheese and wine on the quays.

items.n: Jazz in a Latin Quarter cave
items.d: Swing dancing in a medieval cellar.
Watch PSG at the Parc des Princes, one of Europe's most intense atmospheres.
Parisian cabaret: the Crazy Horse's artistic shows or the Lido's new musical productions.
Croissants or macarons with a chef.
Tour Paris in a convertible Citroën 2CV with a local driver, including night tours.
The 11th arrondissement is the epicentre of Paris's natural-wine bar scene, like Le Baron Rouge.
A famously long queue in the Marais for a pita stuffed with falafel, aubergine and tahini.
Crisp-crusted baguette from an award-winning bakery.
Duck legs slow-cooked in their own fat until crisp, served with sautéed potatoes. A southwest classic.
Chicken braised in red wine with lardons and mushrooms. Burgundy's comfort food.
A thin, crispy chickpea pancake cooked in wood ovens and served in paper cones at Nice's market.
Lorraine gave the world the quiche and the shell-shaped madeleine cake.
A Breton pastry of layered butter and sugar, caramelised to crispy perfection.
Buy oysters from stalls by the harbour and eat them on the sea wall with views of Mont-Saint-Michel bay.
Many starred restaurants offer set lunch menus at a fraction of the dinner price.
Markets at L'Isle-sur-la-Sorgue and Uzès.
Tour Hennessy, Rémy Martin or Martell in Cognac and taste aged brandies.
Crisp, mineral Chardonnay from northern Burgundy's oyster-fossil soils.
Breton cider poured into ceramic bowls alongside crêpes.
Herbal liqueur made by Carthusian monks in the Alps using a secret recipe of 130 herbs. Tour the cellars at Voiron.
A medieval Normandy city with the Gothic cathedral Monet painted 30 times and the site of Joan of Arc's execution.
A walled medieval town of half-timbered houses above the River Rance in Brittany.
Breton capital with faience pottery.
Strange pink boulders sculpted by the sea at Ploumanac'h, with a coastal path.
A Loire château town where Leonardo da Vinci spent his last years at the Clos Lucé.
A lively university city and convenient base for the châteaux, with a medieval old town.
Famous for its Renaissance gardens with geometric vegetable beds and ornamental hedges.
Hilltop wine village with a monolithic church.
A royal town with a Boulevard des Pyrénées panorama of the whole mountain chain.
Pilgrimage town; candlelight procession.
A mountain-top observatory at 2,877 m; stay overnight for stargazing.
The pink-brick city of the southwest, home to Airbus and the Cité de l'espace.
Watch huge airliners being assembled in Toulouse. Book in advance; bring passport ID.
Red-brick cathedral and Toulouse-Lautrec.
A Gothic hilltop village that seems to float above the morning fog.
The world's tallest bridge, its masts rising 343 m over the Tarn valley.
A colourful Catalan fishing port that inspired Matisse and Derain's Fauvism.
A Roman city with a remarkably preserved arena and the temple of Maison Carrée.
A lively student city with a grand Place de la Comédie and beaches nearby.
Cliff village and immersive art quarry.
A Provençal town of canals and water wheels with France's biggest antiques market on Sundays.
A cliff village known for its faience pottery and a gold star hanging over the gorge on a chain.
A small fishing port with pastel houses and boat trips into the calanques.
The asylum where Van Gogh painted The Starry Night, plus the Roman ruins of Glanum.
A pastel harbour on one of the Riviera's deepest bays, between Nice and Monaco.
An Italian-feeling town of lemon trees and pastel houses on the border.
Perfume capital; make your own scent.
Tour de France "Giant of Provence."
Float over Chenonceau and Amboise at dawn.
Rent a self-drive boat on the 17th-century canal lined with plane trees.
A chain of extinct volcanoes; climb the Puy de Dôme or take the panoramic train.
Bird park with thousands of pink flamingos in the Camargue wetlands.
France's largest glacier, by train.
The world's most famous film festival in May, with red-carpet premieres on the Croisette.
Run past the Champs-Élysées, Louvre and Eiffel Tower in April.
Watch Stade Toulousain or another top club in France's rugby league.
Sleep in a real château in the Loire, with gardens and candlelit dinners.
Rent a stone farmhouse with a pool among the lavender and vineyards.
The famous avenue and the luxury fashion houses of Avenue Montaigne.
The world's largest antiques market, with more than 1,700 dealers in a maze of alleys.
A legendary English-language bookshop opposite Notre-Dame, with a reading room upstairs.
Green boxes along the Seine selling secondhand books, old posters and prints.
Military parade on the Champs-Élysées and fireworks at the Eiffel Tower.
Free concerts on every street corner.
Beaches along the Seine and canal swimming.
Watch a mountain stage or the finale.
France's surf coast: Biarritz's elegant beaches and Hossegor's powerful beach breaks, host of pro contests.
Purple fields at Valensole and Sénanque Abbey.
Europe's grand canyon, 700 m deep with turquoise water. Kayak or pedal boat from Lac de Sainte-Croix.
A former fishing village turned jet-set port, with Pampelonne beach clubs and the Sénéquier café.
Swim the Med from Villefranche to Saint-Tropez.
Europe's toughest long-distance trail.
170 km trek through France, Italy and Switzerland.
One of the world's top paragliding sites; tandem flights from Col de la Forclaz land by the lake.
The world's most famous endurance race, held in June, with fans camping around the circuit.
Clouds boiling up over Mont Blanc and thunder echoing through the valley. Watch from a café terrace.
Endless yellow fields in the southwest and Provence.

items.n: Midsummer evening on the Canal Saint-Martin
items.d: Parisians picnicking on the canal edges at 22:00 light.
Tractors cutting rows of purple with the scent everywhere.
Provençal summer classics in Nice: vegetable stew and salad with tuna, eggs and olives.
The aniseed apéritif of the south, diluted with water until it turns cloudy. Pair with pétanque.
Taste pale, dry rosé at the estates where it's made, around Saint-Tropez and the Var.
Deauville's chic boardwalk and casino and Trouville's fish market across the river.
Sail the Gulf of Morbihan's 40 islands and visit wild Belle-Île.

items.n: La Rochelle and Île de Ré
items.d: La Rochelle's medieval harbour towers and the cycling island of Île de Ré, with salt marshes.
A Basque fishing port with a sandy bay, tuna boats and red-and-white houses.
1,500 m amphitheatre of cliffs and waterfalls.
Swim in one of Europe's cleanest lakes, at beaches like Plage d'Albigny.
Car-free ski resort; mountain biking in summer.
Cycle the 21 hairpins made famous by the Tour de France.
Paddle 30 km through the gorge, passing under the Pont d'Arc stone arch, and camp on the riverbank.
Drift past castles and cliff villages like La Roque-Gageac on a gentle river.
A coast-to-coast trail across the Pyrenees. Do a section like the Cirque de Gavarnie.
Climb iron ladders and cables on cliffs around Chamonix and Annecy.
The island's wild west coast of cliffs and needles, painted by Monet.
An alpine lake reflecting Mont Blanc, about 2.5 hours' hike above Chamonix.
A deep limestone canyon with cliff villages, best explored by canoe.
Avignon's July theatre festival, plus the sprawling Off festival with hundreds of shows.
Opera performed in a perfectly preserved Roman theatre in Orange.
A huge celebration of Celtic music and culture with bagpipes from all Celtic nations.
Five days of street partying in white and red with bulls, music and processions.
Spend a night in an Alpine hut with shared dinners and sunrise on the peaks.
Rich onion soup topped with bread and bubbling Gruyère. The old Les Halles market workers' breakfast.
Thick "l'Africain" chocolate since 1903.
On the first Saturday in October, museums, churches and public spaces host free all-night art installations.
Apple brandy, cider and Camembert country.
Slow-cooked beans with duck confit and sausage.
On the third Thursday of November, the year's first wine is released with festivities in Beaujolais and in bars everywhere.
Beef braised slowly in red Burgundy wine with mushrooms, onions and bacon.
Riesling and Gewürztraminer villages.
Château towers rising above a sea of morning mist.
The Côte d'Or turns yellow and copper after harvest.
Waves crashing on the lighthouse at Pointe du Raz.
Golden chestnut woods and roasting stalls.

items.n: Musée de Montmartre and the vineyard
items.d: Renoir's old studio and gardens overlooking Paris's last working vineyard, harvested each October.
Mashed potatoes beaten with Tomme cheese until stretchy, from the Aubrac plateau.
A Rhône wine village under a ruined papal castle, home of powerful red blends.
A Basque village where red peppers hang drying on the house façades; pepper festival in October.
Europe's biggest flea market, two million visitors in a weekend, and mussels and fries everywhere.
Villages celebrate the vendanges with parades, tastings and dances.

items.n: Paris Christmas lights and department stores
items.d: Galeries Lafayette's giant tree and window displays.
The Périgord's winter treasures. Visit a truffle market (Dec–Feb) and a foie gras farm.
One of the world's biggest carnivals, with flower battles where costumed performers throw mimosa to the crowd.
Giant sculptures made from tonnes of oranges and lemons in the Biovès gardens each February.
Four nights around December 8 when Lyon's buildings are lit by light artists and residents place candles in windows.
One of Europe's oldest Christmas markets.
A legendary 20 km off-piste descent across glaciers from the Aiguille du Midi to Chamonix. A guide is essential.
Alpine cheese feasts: melted raclette scraped over potatoes, and fondue made with Beaufort and Comté.
Potatoes, onions and bacon baked under a whole Reblochon cheese. The ultimate après-ski dish.

items.w: Rare; a few days in Jan–Feb
items.d: Sacré-Cœur's steps under fresh snow and an empty Place du Tertre.
Lunch outdoors at 15°C with snow-capped Alps behind.
Waking up to 50 cm of fresh snow in Val d'Isère.
Epiphany cake with a hidden figurine.
A Christmas log cake of sponge and buttercream, decorated like a tree trunk.
A chic old ski village founded by the Rothschilds, with horse-drawn sleighs.

items.n: Ice skating at the Hôtel de Ville
items.d: Paris's free seasonal ice rink in front of the City Hall.
A boisterous carnival where costumed crowds sing and the mayor throws herring from the town hall.
Riquewihr, Kaysersberg and Eguisheim become storybook Christmas villages.

countries.name: Monaco
countries.intro: A 2 km² city-state of yachts, casinos and Formula 1, easily combined with Nice.

sp.text: Monaco Grand Prix (late May/early June) and the Historic GP in even years. Pleasant before summer crowds.

su.text: Beach clubs, superyachts, the fireworks festival, peak glamour and prices.

fa.text: Monaco Yacht Show in late September; warm sea into October.

wi.text: Monte-Carlo Rally (January), mild, quiet, Christmas village on the port.

items.w: Dress code in the evening; daytime visits allowed
items.d: The Belle Époque casino by Charles Garnier. Visit the gaming rooms by day, or play in the evening (dress code applies, passport required).
Changing of the guard daily at 11:55.
A white-stone cathedral where Grace Kelly and Prince Rainier are buried.
Cliff-top aquarium founded by Prince Albert I.
Superyacht harbour and F1 paddock area.
Walk the hairpin, tunnel and Swimming Pool section.
The jewel of Formula 1. Grandstand or yacht-terrace tickets sell out.
A clay-court tennis tournament in April at the Monte-Carlo Country Club, overlooking the sea.
A cliffside garden of cacti and succulents, with a cave below. Check reopening status after renovations.

items.k: Collection de Voitures du Prince de Monaco
items.d: Prince Rainier III's collection of more than 100 cars, from vintage models to Formula 1 cars.
Monaco's fried pastries filled with chard and ricotta.
People-watching beside the casino, as supercars circle Casino Square.
Superyachts lit up below the casino, seen from the Prince's Palace terrace.
F1 cars screaming through the streets, the sound bouncing around the amphitheatre of buildings.
Pastel lanes and squares on the clifftop.
Shady clifftop gardens on the Rock with views over the sea.
A peaceful Zen garden by the sea, designed by Yasuo Beppu. Free entry.
Grand hotel with Louis XV restaurant.
Garnier's opera house inside the casino.
Electric racing on the street circuit.

items.n: Stade Louis II and AS Monaco
items.d: Watch AS Monaco in Ligue 1 or the Champions League in a stadium with arches.
A seven-minute flight from Nice Airport to Monaco's heliport, with views of the coast.
Monaco nightlife: dinner at Buddha-Bar, then dance at the famous Jimmy'z nightclub.
Stay in the Belle Époque Hermitage or at the Fairmont, above the famous Grand Prix hairpin.
Luxury boutiques and jewellers around the casino gardens.
Monaco's free public beach, recently renovated, with beach clubs and clear water.
Outdoor concerts in the Prince's Palace courtyard.
Concerts by international stars in the Salle des Étoiles in July and August.
The world's top superyacht show in late September, with more than 100 superyachts in Port Hercule.
Waves breaking over the harbour walls and the sea turning slate-grey.
November 19: a Mass, a parade and the princely family on the palace balcony.
World Rally Championship opener in the Alps.
Lunch outside in January with the Alps snow-capped behind the harbour.
The world's most prestigious circus festival in January, with the Golden Clown awards.
Burning of a boat in front of the church.

countries.name: Belgium
countries.intro: Small country, huge on flavour: beer, chocolate, waffles and fries, plus medieval Flemish cities and WWI history.

sp.text: Royal Greenhouses of Laeken open (Apr–May), Hallerbos bluebells, carnival at Binche (Feb–Mar).

su.text: Flower Carpet (August, even years), Tomorrowland, terrace beer season.

fa.text: Hunting-season game dishes, Ypres remembrance, cosy brown cafés.

wi.text: Christmas markets in Brussels, Bruges and Ghent; Binche Carnival; mussels season.

items.d: The EU capital with Art Nouveau architecture and comic-strip murals.
Brussels' central square, ringed by gilded guildhalls and the Gothic town hall. Often called the most beautiful square in Europe; spectacular lit up at night.
A tiny bronze statue of a boy peeing into a fountain. He has more than 1,000 costumes and is dressed up several times a week.
A 102 m model of an iron crystal built for the 1958 World's Fair. Ride up to the top sphere for views and an exhibition on the Expo.
The world's largest collection of René Magritte's surrealist paintings, drawings and photos, part of the Royal Museums of Fine Arts.
Belgium's comic-strip museum, with Tintin and the Smurfs, in an Art Nouveau department store by Victor Horta.
Architect Victor Horta's own house and studio, a masterpiece of Art Nouveau with flowing ironwork, stained glass and a light-filled stairwell.

items.w: Only about three weeks in Apr–May
items.d: A spectacular complex of 19th-century glass greenhouses, open to the public for only about three weeks each spring.
A beech forest near Brussels whose floor turns violet-blue with wild bluebells for about two weeks in late April. Go early on a weekday.
A perfectly preserved medieval city of canals, cobbled lanes, brick gables and swans. Stay overnight to see it empty and lit up.
Climb 366 narrow steps up the 83 m medieval bell tower on the Markt for views over the rooftops, and hear the 47-bell carillon.
A boat trip through Bruges' canals, past the medieval houses and under low bridges.
A lively student city with a castle, canal-side guildhalls and Van Eyck's altarpiece. Less touristy than Bruges.
Van Eyck's Adoration of the Mystic Lamb (1432), one of the most important paintings in the world, in St Bavo's Cathedral.
A medieval castle in the centre of Ghent, with ramparts, a torture museum and views.
Belgium's cool second city: the diamond district, Rubens' house and cathedral, fashion boutiques and a big port.
Often called the world's most beautiful train station, with a marble hall and giant dome, nicknamed the "railway cathedral."
A UNESCO-listed Renaissance printing house with the world's two oldest surviving printing presses.
Two charming university towns with grand Gothic town halls and lively squares.
A riverside town under a cliff-top citadel, the birthplace of Adolphe Sax, inventor of the saxophone.
A tiny medieval town in the Ardennes that calls itself the "world's smallest city," with a castle, a topiary park and cobbled lanes.
Rolling forested hills, river valleys and castles in southern Belgium. Great for hiking, kayaking on the Lesse and cosy inns.
A rebuilt WWI town with a memorial gate where buglers play the Last Post every evening at 20:00.

items.k: Tyne Cot Commonwealth War Graves Cemetery
items.d: The largest Commonwealth war cemetery in the world, with nearly 12,000 graves from WWI's Battle of Passchendaele.
The site of Napoleon's 1815 defeat. Climb the Lion's Mound and visit the museum.
Westvleteren, Chimay, Orval, Rochefort, Westmalle.
A family brewery in Brussels making lambic beer by spontaneous fermentation. Tour it and taste gueuze.
A famous Brussels bar with more than 2,000 beers on its menu, in a lane off the Grand-Place.
Brussels (light) vs Liège (dense and caramelised).
Thick, twice-fried potatoes in a paper cone, from a friterie like Maison Antoine. Belgians claim they invented them.
Taste pralines from Neuhaus, Pierre Marcolini and Mary on the Sablon square.

items.n: Rainy evening in a Bruges brown café
items.d: Rain on the canals while you drink a Brugse Zot by a window.
Mist on the Rozenhoedkaai before the day-trippers.
One of Europe's first covered shopping arcades (1847), with chocolatiers, glovemakers and cafés under a glass roof.
A formal garden on a hillside between the old and upper towns, with a classic view to the town hall spire.
A park with a grand triumphal arch, plus museums of military history, cars and art.
A car museum in a vast hall at the Cinquantenaire, with more than 250 vehicles.
More than 1,000 instruments in a striking Art Nouveau building, with a rooftop café.
A free museum that tells the story of Europe in the 20th century.
The European Parliament's free visitor centre, explaining how the EU works.
A chapel in Bruges holding a phial said to contain Christ's blood, shown daily.
A peaceful walled courtyard of white houses where Benedictine nuns live, carpeted with daffodils in spring.
A horse-drawn carriage tour through the medieval streets.
Ghent's guildhall quays are beautifully lit at night, a highlight of the city's lighting plan.
A crusader castle on a rocky ridge, with falconry shows in summer.
A huge cave system reached by an old tram, with a wildlife park on top.
Belgium's highest point: a raised peat bog crossed by boardwalks, often snowy in winter.
Cycling is a passion here. Watch the Tour of Flanders in April or a muddy winter cyclocross race.
Cycle flat paths through Flemish fields, canals and villages.
Deep-fried croquettes filled with grey North Sea shrimp in a creamy sauce.
Cone-shaped purple raspberry candies with a soft centre, sold from stalls in Ghent.
Learn to make pralines and mendiants with a Belgian chocolatier.
Brewed by Trappist monks and often called the world's best beer. Drink it at the abbey café In de Vrede.
Ruins of a medieval abbey beside a working Trappist monastery that brews Orval beer.
Kwak beer served in a round-bottomed glass in a wooden stand, originally for coachmen.
Bruges' UNESCO-listed procession on Ascension Day, with biblical scenes.

items.w: Every three years in May; check the next date
items.d: Ypres' Kattenstoet, a parade with giant cat figures held every three years in May.
A UNESCO-listed festival in Mons where St George battles a dragon in front of a cheering crowd.
Free jazz across the city in May.
In mid-August of even years, a huge carpet of begonias covers the Grand-Place.
Ten days of free music, theatre and street parties in July, one of Europe's largest city festivals.
The world's biggest electronic music festival, held in Boom each July.
The Belgian Grand Prix at one of F1's best-loved tracks, famous for the Eau Rouge–Raidillon corner and unpredictable weather.
The official palace, open in summer, with a Mirror Room whose ceiling is covered with jewel beetle wings.
A seaside city with a long promenade, fish market and art museum. Belgium's coastal capital.
A Belle Époque seaside resort with half-timbered villas, dunes and a sandy beach.
A Renaissance pageant on the Grand-Place each July, re-enacting a 1549 procession.
A beer festival on the Grand-Place in September.
A pot of steamed mussels with fries, cooked in white wine, celery and onion. Best between July and April.
Beef stewed slowly in dark Belgian beer with onions and spiced bread, served with fries.
In October, the beech forests of the Ardennes turn gold and copper, with mist in the river valleys.

items.n: North Sea wind on the coast tram
items.d: The world's longest tram line along a blustery coast.
Mashed potato with vegetables like carrots or leeks, served with sausage. Brussels comfort food.
A creamy chicken or fish stew from Ghent, with vegetables and potatoes.
Brussels' Christmas market stretches from the Bourse to Place Sainte-Catherine, with a Ferris wheel, ice rink and light show on the Grand-Place.
A UNESCO-listed carnival where Gilles in wax masks and ostrich-feather hats dance and throw oranges.
Spiced caramelised shortcrust biscuits, eaten year-round and traditionally on St Nicholas Day.
The gilded guildhalls dusted with rare snow.
A February festival with hundreds of Belgian beers.

items.w: Held every few years in early February; check dates
items.d: Light art installations around Ghent, held every few years in winter.

countries.name: Netherlands
countries.intro: Canals, bikes, tulips, windmills and masterpieces by Rembrandt and Van Gogh, all connected by excellent trains.

sp.text: Tulip season (late Mar–mid May), Keukenhof, King's Day (Apr 27). The best season.

su.text: Beaches at Scheveningen, festivals, Pride in early August. Busy and pricey.

fa.text: Amsterdam Dance Event in October, fewer crowds, cosy brown cafés.

wi.text: Amsterdam Light Festival, Sinterklaas (Dec 5), skating if canals freeze, oliebollen.

items.d: A Golden Age city of canals, gabled houses, world-class museums and more bikes than people.
The national museum, with Rembrandt's Night Watch, Vermeer's Milkmaid and Delft Blue pottery.
The world's largest collection of Van Gogh's paintings, including Sunflowers. Book a time slot.

items.w: Tickets released online six weeks ahead
items.d: The canal house where Anne Frank hid for two years. Walk through the Secret Annex behind the movable bookcase.
See the UNESCO-listed canal ring from the water on a glass-roofed boat or a small open boat.
A charming neighbourhood of narrow canals, brown cafés, galleries and markets.
Amsterdam's biggest park, with ponds, an open-air theatre and cafés.
Rent a bike and join the locals on the city's cycle lanes, crossing canals and visiting neighbourhoods.
Ride to the top of the A'DAM Tower and swing out over the edge, 100 m above the IJ river.
On April 27, the whole country wears orange. Amsterdam becomes a city-wide flea market and street party.
A 32-hectare park with seven million bulbs in bloom from late March to mid-May.
Bike through stripes of tulips, daffodils and hyacinths around Lisse.
Historic windmills, clog makers and cheese farms close to Amsterdam.
A UNESCO-listed line of 19 windmills built in the 1700s to drain the polders.
A village without roads: thatched cottages connected by canals and wooden bridges. Rent a whisper boat.
A university city with unique two-level canals and wharf cellars turned into cafés.
A canal town famous for blue-and-white pottery and as Vermeer's home.
The seat of government, with the Peace Palace, the Mauritshuis and Scheveningen beach.
A small museum with Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring and Rembrandt.
A modern port city of bold architecture: the Cube Houses, Markthal and Erasmus Bridge.
A beautiful town near Amsterdam with the Frans Hals Museum and a huge market square.
A lively southern city with bastions, caves and fine dining near Belgium.
Fishing villages with traditional costumes and wooden houses.
A huge park of forest, heath and sand dunes with free white bikes and the Kröller-Müller Museum.
Thin waffles with caramel syrup in the middle. Eat them fresh from a market stall.
Crispy fried balls of beef ragout, served with mustard as a bar snack.
Tiny, fluffy pancakes with butter and powdered sugar.
A colonial-era banquet of 10–20 small Indonesian dishes with rice.
In Alkmaar, carriers in white suits carry cheeses on sledges in a traditional market each Friday morning in summer.
Dutch gin served in a tulip glass, filled to the brim, at a 300-year-old tasting room like Wynand Fockink.
Drops dimpling the canals, bikes clattering by, then a jenever in a brown café.
Stripes of red, yellow and pink from a plane or balloon.
The towering clouds painted by Ruisdael, over flat polders.
Climb Amsterdam's tallest church tower, next to Anne Frank House, for views over the canals.
A hidden courtyard of 14th-century houses in the heart of Amsterdam, with a wooden house from 1528.
The 17th-century former town hall on Dam Square, now a royal palace with grand marble halls.
Nine little streets crossing the canal ring, packed with boutiques, vintage shops and cafés.
A flower market on floating barges selling tulip bulbs and souvenirs.
An old shipyard turned creative zone with street art, studios and a huge monthly flea market.
The national museum of modern art and design, with Mondrian and Rietveld.
A small museum of modern art in a townhouse, with works by Banksy and Warhol.
A secret Catholic church hidden in the attic of a 17th-century canal house.
A tour through the old Heineken brewery, ending in a tasting.
M.C. Escher's mind-bending works in a former royal winter palace.
A huge collection of Van Gogh paintings in a museum within the Hoge Veluwe forest, with a sculpture garden.
A mirrored bowl-shaped art storage building you can explore, with a rooftop forest.
Tilted yellow cube houses on poles by Piet Blom. Visit the show cube.
A huge arched food hall with a giant painted ceiling and apartments above.
A white cable-stayed bridge nicknamed "The Swan," Rotterdam's landmark.
The Netherlands' tallest church tower (112 m) in Utrecht; 465 steps to the top.
The largest castle in the Netherlands, a neo-Gothic fairy tale with gardens.
A miniature park of the Netherlands' top sights at 1:25 scale.
A 32 km dyke closing off the former Zuiderzee, with a monument and visitor centre.
Massive storm-surge barriers built after the 1953 flood. Visit at Neeltje Jans.
A canal-filled university town where Rembrandt was born and the Pilgrims lived.
A town with a cheese market in summer, a Gothic town hall and candle night in December.
A quiet village with a summer cheese market and canals.
A lively student city in the north with a Martini Tower.
A Burgundian town with Hieronymus Bosch's legacy and chocolate-covered Bossche bollen.
A 13th-century moated castle near Amsterdam with towers and gardens.
A peninsula of green wooden houses and a historic harbour town.

items.n: Rent a boat on the canals
items.d: Rent an electric boat, no licence needed, and cruise the canals yourself.
Cycle through coastal dunes near Haarlem, where Scottish Highland cattle graze.
Borrow free white bikes and ride through forest, dunes and heath.
A rescue centre for injured seals on the Wadden Sea coast.
A nature reserve with wild horses, deer and birds.
Thick fries with mayo; "patatje oorlog" adds peanut sauce and onions.
Battered cod bites with garlic sauce from a fish stall.
Deep-dish apple pie with whipped cream at Winkel 43.
Chocolate sprinkles on buttered bread. A Dutch breakfast.
A wall of hot snacks behind little glass doors, like croquettes and frikandel.
A traditional pub with wood panelling and nicotine-stained walls, like Café 't Smalle.
An organic brewery next to a windmill, with a busy terrace.
May 5: free music festivals celebrating the end of WWII occupation.
Floats covered in flowers parade from Noordwijk to Haarlem in April.
Amsterdam's most famous street market, with stroopwafels, herring and cheese.
Canal Parade of decorated boats, the world's only floating Pride.
Texel and Terschelling; mudflat walking (wadlopen).
Walk across the Wadden Sea seabed at low tide with a guide.
Raw herring eaten whole by the tail, with onions and pickles. New-season herring arrives in June.
In June, Amsterdammers take their small boats out with drinks until 22:00 light.
A province of islands and beaches with seafood and oysters.
The largest Wadden island, with beaches, dunes, sheep and seals.
Take a kitesurfing lesson on the wide North Sea beach in The Hague.
In August, the Veluwe heathlands turn purple with blooming heather.
A month of theatre, dance and music in Amsterdam each June.
One of the world's biggest jazz festivals, in July.
The world's biggest club festival, five days in October.

items.n: Windy cycling against a North Sea gale
items.d: Locals ride into headwinds; there are even championships for it.

items.n: Autumn storm on the beach at Scheveningen
items.d: Kite surfers and wild sea during autumn storms.
The windmills appearing out of the morning mist.
The world's largest flower parade, with giant floats covered in dahlias, in September.
A light-art festival that transforms the streets of Eindhoven each November.
Light art along the canals, best seen from a boat cruise.
Skating on frozen canals and lakes is a Dutch dream, possible only in rare hard frosts.
St Nicholas arrives by boat in mid-November; families exchange gifts on December 5.
Three days of costumes, brass bands and parties in February.
Deep-fried dough balls with raisins, eaten at New Year.
The whole country skating on the ditches and canals.
An ice rink in front of the Rijksmuseum in winter.
Thick pea soup with smoked sausage, a winter staple.

countries.name: Luxembourg
countries.intro: Tiny Grand Duchy with a gorge-split capital, castles, Moselle wine and free public transport nationwide.

sp.text: Hiking the Mullerthal, Emaischen pottery market (Easter Monday).

su.text: National Day (Jun 23), Schueberfouer funfair late Aug.

fa.text: Moselle wine harvest and festivals.

wi.text: Winterlights Christmas market, quiet castles.

items.d: A capital built on cliffs over deep gorges, with a UNESCO old town and fortifications.
17 km of tunnels carved into the rock beneath the old fortress, used as shelters during both World Wars. Open March to November.
A ramparts walkway called "Europe's most beautiful balcony," overlooking the Grund quarter and the Alzette valley.
A riverside quarter at the base of the gorge, with old stone houses, an abbey and pubs, reached by a free lift.
A restored hilltop castle with a chairlift and great views.
A 112 km trail through "Little Switzerland," with sandstone gorges, mossy forests and narrow rock passages.
Luxembourg's oldest town, with a Benedictine abbey and the UNESCO-listed hopping procession on Whit Tuesday.
Luxembourg's national dish: smoked pork collar with broad beans and potatoes.
All buses, trams and trains in Luxembourg are free.
In April, vineyards and orchards along the Moselle wake up with blossom.
A Gothic cathedral with the crypt of the Grand Ducal family.
A stone arch bridge with a cycle deck slung underneath.
A glass lift linking the upper city with the Pfaffenthal valley.
A modern art museum by I.M. Pei in a fortress setting.
Medieval ruins next to a Renaissance castle, with blackcurrant liqueur.
A hilltop castle ruin with views over the Sûre valley.
The village where the Schengen Agreement was signed, with a museum.
Dioramas and vehicles from the Battle of the Bulge.
A WWII cemetery where General George S. Patton is buried.
A small Ardennes town whose castle holds The Family of Man, a famous UNESCO-listed photo exhibition.
A waterfall under a stone bridge in the Mullerthal.
A two-week Catholic pilgrimage to the cathedral in spring, with a market of stalls.
An Easter Monday market selling bird-shaped clay whistles.
Flour dumplings served with bacon bits and cream. Hearty Luxembourg comfort food.
Sparkling wine made in the champagne method from Moselle grapes. Tour a cellar in Grevenmacher.
June 23: the Grand Duke's birthday celebrated with fireworks and parties.
A 700-year-old funfair in late August and September.
The Grand Duke's official residence in the old town, open for guided tours in July and August.
A reservoir lake in the Ardennes with clean water for swimming, kayaking and paddleboarding.
A wine route along the Moselle, with crémant and Riesling tastings.
On autumn mornings, mist fills the gorge so the old town seems to float above the clouds.
A September wine festival along the Moselle where wineries open their doors for tastings.
